first_reader_source: Version of record: Drug Testing and Analysis 2024;16(9):942–947, doi 10.1002/dta.3612
title: Understanding sensitivity and cross-reactivity of xylazine lateral flow immunoassay test strips for drug checking applications

claims.statement: In the studies read, a test that showed one drug did not show what else was in the sample or how much drug it held, and no study measured whether a negative result means a sample is less risky. A colour kit read by experienced analysts gave the same positive MDMA reading for seven samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA as for samples of MDMA alone (Murray et al., 2003). In drug-checking samples in the Vancouver area, 24 of 159 contained a newer benzodiazepine that the person had not expected (most expected fentanyl), 17 of them also held fentanyl, and infrared spectroscopy, which can identify several components, listed fentanyl in only 3 of those 17 and a benzodiazepine in 2 of the 24 (editors' count from the paper's table; Laing et al., 2021). Each strip type reacts to one drug or family and missed related drugs in laboratory tests: xylazine strips did not react to medetomidine or several other sedatives (Sisco et al., 2024a), and nitazene, fentanyl and benzodiazepine strips missed some nitazenes, fentanyl analogues and etizolam (see the answers on each strip). Fentanyl strips are built to show presence only, not concentration, purity or which analogue (Green et al., 2020); in pure solutions the test band became fainter as the fentanyl concentration rose, but the makers' rule reads only whether a band is there (Bergh et al., 2021), no study read tested whether a line's strength shows how much drug a sample holds, and a scoping review lists that belief among mistaken ones (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand). Authors of three studies state that a negative result does not mean a drug is safe and that a positive one gives no amount (De Vrieze et al., 2024; Sisco et al., 2024a; Winstock et al., 2001); these are their conclusions, not tested findings. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Murray et al.: 7 of 35 MDMA samples held a second drug, all read like MDMA alone. Laing et al.: 24/159 samples held an NPS benzodiazepine (15.1%), none expected; 17 of 24 also held fentanyl; FTIR listed fentanyl in 3 of those 17 and an NPS benzodiazepine in 2 of 24 (editors' count from Table 2). Sisco et al. (2024a): medetomidine and four α2-agonists did not react at 100 µg/mL. Amount: no study read tested whether strips or colour tests estimate amount.

claims.statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, detected xylazine reliably when there was at least the strip's listed amount and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not, so these strips would not show them (Sisco et al., 2024a). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Sisco et al. (2024a), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). Pure xylazine: 15/15 positive at 2.5 µg/mL and above; 3/15 at 1 µg/mL (12 faint); 7/15 at 0.5 µg/mL (8 faint); 0/15 at 0.1 µg/mL. Cross-reactivity at 100 µg/mL: lidocaine only of 76 other compounds. Sisco et al. (2024b), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.
